name: kyoto-cabinet
desc: Library of routines for managing a database
why: A compact key-value database with an old-school design, a rewarding look at how embedded stores work underneath.

brief.what_it_is: Kyoto Cabinet is a library for managing a database that is a single simple data file of records, each a key-value pair. Keys and values are variable-length byte strings, and either binary data or text can be used for either. Records are organized in a hash table or a B+ tree, and each key must be unique within a database. It has no concept of data tables or data types. It is written in C++ and offered as an API for C, Java, Python, Ruby, Perl, and Lua, and the homepage also links specifications for command line utilities.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a straightforward implementation of DBM, aimed at fast, small, and scalable key-value storage. The author claims storing one million records takes 0.9 seconds for the hash database and 1.1 seconds for the B+ tree database, with overhead of 16 bytes per record for hash and 4 bytes for B+ tree.
brief.how_it_works: Records are stored in a single data file and indexed either by a hash table or a B+ tree, chosen when the database is used. Keys must be unique, and values are plain byte strings with no schema. The homepage gives no further internals.
brief.install_notes: The homepage points to source packages for the C/C++ core and for each language binding, binary packages for Windows (C/C++/Java), and says other binary packages come from each platform's distributor. It requires a platform with a C++03 API plus TR1 library extensions. No accounts, runtimes beyond that, or first-run configuration appear on the homepage. The brew formula's executables list (kcutilmgr, kchashmgr, kctreemgr and several test programs) is from the package metadata, not from the homepage.
brief.standout: It is a small, old-school embedded store where the same data file can be used with either a hash or a B+ tree, and the homepage quantifies per-record overhead directly. The author also openly points readers to a successor project, Tkrzw, instead of pitching this one as the newest option.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage shows 'Last Update: Fri, 04 Mar 2011' and copyright 2009-2012, and the author says 'There's a successor: Tkrzw.  I recommend you to try it.' I did not check a repository or release history, so no later release date is known.
brief.caveats: The author recommends the successor Tkrzw over this project. The homepage was last updated in March 2011, and its performance figures are the author's own claims. Building from source needs a C++03 compiler with TR1 extensions. The brew formula has no caveats. The README and docs for the command line tools were not fetched, so the commands list is empty.
quotes: Kyoto Cabinet is a library of routines for managing a database.
There's a successor: Tkrzw.  I recommend you to try it.
